name: Hanging Hearts
description: Pak Chanek has $$$n$$$ blank heart-shaped cards. Card $$$1$$$ is attached directly to the wall while each of the other cards is hanging onto exactly one other card by a piece of string. Specifically, card $$$i$$$ ($$$i \gt 1$$$) is hanging onto card $$$p_i$$$ ($$$p_i \lt i$$$). In the very beginning, Pak Chanek must write one integer number on each card. He does this by choosing any permutation $$$a$$$ of $$$[1, 2, \dots, n]$$$. Then, the number written on card $$$i$$$ is $$$a_i$$$. After that, Pak Chanek must do the following operation $$$n$$$ times while maintaining a sequence $$$s$$$ (which is initially empty): Choose a card $$$x$$$ such that no other cards are hanging onto it. Append the number written on card $$$x$$$ to the end of $$$s$$$. If $$$x \neq 1$$$ and the number on card $$$p_x$$$ is larger than the number on card $$$x$$$, replace the number on card $$$p_x$$$ with the number on card $$$x$$$. Remove card $$$x$$$. After that, Pak Chanek will have a sequence $$$s$$$ with $$$n$$$ elements. What is the maximum length of the longest non-decreasing subsequence$$$^\dagger$$$ of $$$s$$$ at the end if Pak Chanek does all the steps optimally? $$$^\dagger$$$ A sequence $$$b$$$ is a subsequence of a sequence $$$c$$$ if $$$b$$$ can be obtained from $$$c$$$ by deletion of several (possibly, zero or all) elements. For example, $$$[3,1]$$$ is a subsequence of $$$[3,2,1]$$$, $$$[4,3,1]$$$ and $$$[3,1]$$$, but not $$$[1,3,3,7]$$$ and $$$[3,10,4]$$$.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 10^5$$$) — the number of heart-shaped cards. The second line contains $$$n - 1$$$ integers $$$p_2, p_3, \dots, p_n$$$ ($$$1 \le p_i \lt i$$$) describing which card that each card hangs onto.
output_specification: Print a single integer — the maximum length of the longest non-decreasing subsequence of $$$s$$$ at the end if Pak Chanek does all the steps optimally.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1740E — Hanging Hearts [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
